submission.natural_language_explanation: Severance-phrase detector: the positive pole fires on the token that completes an expression of cutting or severing, above all the particle ' off' (or the closed forms 'cutoff'/'cut-off'/'cutoffs'/'crosscut') when the verb is a form of cut (4.9-8.4 of the 6.1 max), and more weakly after other blade or detachment verbs such as chop, clip, trim, slice, crop, hack, lop, snip, sever, rip, tear, break, bite, chip, snap, twist, chew, crush, slash or mince (1.4-4.1, but not saw/prune/shave/peel/amputate off); the same completing role is played by ' short' after cut ('cut it short', 3.8), the ' section'/' sections' of 'cross section'/'cross-sectional' (3.3-3.7), and Chinese severance words (截止 3.1-6.0, 截 4.1, 截断 6.6, 截取 3.7, 割断 2.7, 剪断 1.8). The same tokens outside such a frame stay near baseline (<1.0: ' off' after turn/take/set/pay/sign/log/call/push/lift/wash/peel, 'a short story', 'the section of the report', 停止/结束/中断), while the object slot right after cut already reads 1.9 ('cut it') and 2.7 when 'Cut' opens the text, so only activity above about 2 is severance-specific.

rival_explanations: Narrow reading: the pole is keyed to the single English verb 'cut' plus its particle 'off' (and closed forms cutoff/cut-off), so it should fire on 'cut ... off' anywhere but not on chop/clip/trim/slice + off, 截止/截断, or 'cross section'.

Collocation-memory reading: the pole merely completes any frequent fixed two-word unit already begun in context (cut off, cross section, cut short, of course, New York), so it is phrase memory rather than severance and should fire on 'course' after 'of' and 'York' after 'New'.

Subword-compound reading: the pole fires on the second element of any compound word or non-initial subword piece regardless of meaning (off in cut-off, section in cross-section, Short in moduleShortSuffix, pt in ceptor), so it should fire equally on well-known, e-mail and text-decoration.

Hemmema

A hemmema (from Finnish "Hämeenmaa", Tavastia) was a type of warship built for the Swedish archipelago fleet and the Russian Baltic navy in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. The hemmema was initially developed for use against the Russian Navy in the Archipelago Sea and along the coasts of Svealand and Finland. It was designed by the prolific and innovative Swedish naval architect Fredrik Henrik af Chapman (1721 – 1808) in collaboration with Augustin Ehrensvärd (1710 – 1772), an artillery officer and later commander of the Swedish archipelago fleet. The hemmema was a specialized vessel for use in the shallow waters and narrow passages that surround the thousands of islands and islets extending from the Swedish capital of Stockholm into the Gulf of Finland.

The hemmema replaced the galleys that had made up the core of the Swedish archipelago fleets until the mid-18th century. Compared to galleys, the hemmema had a deeper draft and was slower under oars, but offered superior accommodation for the crew, carried more stores, was more seaworthy and had roughly ten times as many heavy guns. It could be propelled by either sails or oars but was still smaller and more maneuverable than most sailing warships, which made it suitable for operations in confined waters.

Between 1764 and 1809, Sweden built six hemmemas. The hemmema became the largest and most heavily armed vessel in the archipelago fleet and served in the Russo-Swedish War of 1788 – 90. Oden, the first hemmema, was relatively small and very similar to a turuma, a different type of "archipelago frigate". Russia built six hemmemas based on the Swedish design between 1808 and 1823 after capturing three of the Swedish vessels at the surrender of Sveaborg in 1808. The later versions, both Swedish and Russian, were much larger and much more heavily armed than Oden.

Background

Russian Tsar Peter the Great had established a new capital and powerful naval base in Saint Petersburg in 1703. Russian naval power in the Baltic grew to challenge the interests of Sweden, the other leading power in the Baltic. Swedish holdings at that time included territory in Northern Germany, all of modern Finland and most of the Baltic states, a dominion depending on, and connected by, the Baltic Sea trade routes. During the Great Northern War (1700 – 1721), Sweden lost all its territories in the Baltic states and suffered Russian raids in Finland and along the chain of islands and archipelagos stretching from the Gulf of Finland to Stockholm. The Swedes began to deploy inshore flotillas of shallow-draft vessels, beginning with smaller versions of the traditional Mediterranean galleys. Most of these new vessels were more akin to galiots and were complemented with gun prams. The disastrous war with Russia (1741 – 43) and the minor involvement against Prussia in the Seven Years' War (1757 – 62) showed the need for further expansion and development of the inshore flotillas with more specialized vessels.

# Absolute deviation and standard deviation

## Absolute deviation

The absolute deviation gives information about how close or far a datum is form the other data of the set. Intuitively, we can see one can calculate it as the difference of a value and the average of the data: $$D_i=x_i-\overline{x}$$

We can see that to calculate this deviation, if we know the average, we only need the value which deviation is to be calculated.

Also, we can say that if we have a datum and its absolute deviation, it is possible to isolate the average by applying a simple subtraction:$$\overline{x}=x_i-D_i$$and later we can use it to calculate other deviations.

In a mathematics exam Pedro got $9$, while the average of the class is $6.7$. Calculate the absolute deviation of Pedro's mark.

Applying the formula $$D_i=x_i-\overline{x}=9-6.7=2.3$$

The sign of the absolute deviation shows whether or not the value is above average (positive sign), or below average (negative sign).

The absolute value of the absolute deviation shows how far the value is from the average. A value equal to zero shows that the value is the same as the average, while a high value with regard to other deviations shows that the value is far from the other data.

In a basketball match, we have the following points of the players of a team: $0, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 10, 15, 38$. Calculate the absolute deviation of the scoring of the players of the team.

Applying the formula$$\displaystyle \overline{x}=\frac{0+2+4+5+8+10+10+15+38}{9}=\frac{92}{9}=10.22$$the average is obtained. The deviations can be represented in a table:

First the average is calculated $$\displaystyle \overline{x}=\frac{3\cdot 1+4\cdot 3+5\cdot 4+6\cdot 2+7\cdot 3+9\cdot 1}{1+3+4+2+3+1}=\frac{77}{14}=5.5$$ Next, it is possible to calculate the absolute deviation, including it in the table:

## Standard deviation

Standard deviation is the arithmetical average of the absolute values of the absolute deviations. It is symbolized by $D_{\overline{x}}$ and can be calculated applying the formula$$\displaystyle D_{\overline{x}}=\frac{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{N} |x_i-\overline{x}|}{N}=\frac{|x_1-\overline{x}|+|x_2-\overline{x}|+\ldots+|x_N-\overline{x}|}{N}$$ It shows whether the information is dispersed (or not). High standard deviation involves a lot of changeability in the information, while a standard deviation equal to zero implies that all the values are equal and, therefore, they have the same value as the average.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The utility company threatened to cut off power to the whole neighborhood by Friday morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A novel English 'cut ... off' frame in a utility-billing context unlike the sermon and checklist examples; the hypothesis predicts the ' off' token fires.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Last summer I spent three weeks walking the coastal path in the north. The weather was mostly kind, though the wind never really stopped. Each morning I packed a flask of tea, a bag of nuts and a battered paper map that had been folded and unfolded so often that the creases had begun to tear. The villages along the route were small and quiet, and the people I met were unfailingly generous with directions and with advice about where to find a decent meal. On the eleventh day the path climbed steeply through a stand of pines and then opened onto a wide headland above the sea. I stopped there for a long time, watching the gulls wheel below me and the light change on the water. It was the sort of place that makes you forget how far you have walked. By late afternoon the clouds had gathered and the first rain began to fall, so I quickened my pace toward the next village. The trail descended through wet grass and loose stones, and twice I nearly slipped. I reached the road just before dark. A fallen oak had cut off the lane entirely, and a farmer with a tractor was already working to drag the branches aside. He waved me through his field and pointed out a quicker path to the inn.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Puts 'cut ... off' deep inside a long narrative so a long-context detector is tested rather than a short local window, while keeping the token frame exact.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: First chop off the leafy top of the pineapple, then slice the fruit into thick rings.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A weaker blade verb (chop), moved mid-sentence so it is not split as 'Ch'|'op', completed by ' off'; the hypothesis predicts firing while the narrow 'cut'-only rival predicts none.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The gardener trimmed off the dead blooms and watered the roses along the fence.
adversarial_test_results.detail: trim + off, a verb the hypothesis lists at 1.4-4.1 while the collocation rival has no fixed unit to complete, separating blade meaning from mere frequency.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The meeting was cut short when the fire alarm sounded in the corridor.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The 'cut it short' completion named in the hypothesis, in a new meeting and alarm context; the narrow rival predicts no firing without 'off'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The engineers examined a cross section of the concrete pillar for hairline cracks.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Unhyphenated 'cross section' in an engineering context; the hypothesis predicts the ' section' token fires and the narrow rival predicts it does not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The survey used a cross-sectional design with three hundred adult participants.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hyphenated 'cross-sectional' as an adjective before a noun; the hypothesis predicts the '-sectional' token fires, and the subword rival predicts the same for compound position.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: 本次比赛的报名截止日期已经调整为五月三十一日下午五点。
adversarial_test_results.detail: Chinese 截止 appears as a single token in a deadline notice, one of the hypothesis's claimed Chinese severance words, which the narrow English rival predicts should not fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: 山洪截断了村庄通往外界的唯一道路，救援队只能徒步进入。
adversarial_test_results.detail: Chinese 截断 tokenizes as 截 + 断, so both claimed tokens are present in a flood-cutting-road frame, the hypothesis's strongest Chinese form; only the hypothesis and collocation rivals predict firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The puppy chewed off the corner of the cushion while we were out shopping.
adversarial_test_results.detail: chew + off, a verb far down the hypothesis's list with no fixed English unit for the collocation rival, so only the hypothesis predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Please turn off the lights and lock the back door before you leave.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The same ' off' particle after a switch verb the hypothesis explicitly calls baseline; collocation memory predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The committee will, of course, review the proposal at its next meeting.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A frequent fixed two-word unit with no cutting content, where only the collocation rival predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She moved to New York last spring to start a new job at a bank.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Another frequent fixed unit named by the collocation rival, which the hypothesis predicts stays at baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He published a short story in the campus literary magazine last year.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' short' in its adjective sense, the exact near-miss the hypothesis names as baseline ('a short story').

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Please read the section of the report that covers the annual budget.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' section' in a document sense without 'cross', the hypothesis's own stated baseline ('the section of the report').

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The manager will sign off on the expense report tomorrow morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' off' after sign, listed by the hypothesis as a baseline verb but a frequent collocation the second rival keys on.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She took off her coat and hung it on the hook by the door.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' off' after take, another of the hypothesis's listed baseline verbs whose collocation is very frequent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The picnic was called off because of the heavy snowstorm.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' off' after call, a listed baseline verb with a frequent fixed collocation, so the collocation rival predicts firing and the hypothesis does not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He sawed off the dead branch with a rusty old handsaw.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A blade verb with ' off' that the hypothesis explicitly excludes; the tokenizer splits the verb as 'saw'|'ed' but the excluded frame is still 'saw ... off'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They peeled off the old wallpaper in long damp strips.
adversarial_test_results.detail: ' off' after peel, which the hypothesis explicitly puts out of bounds even though peel is a detachment verb.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Every office has its own small rituals at the end of the day. In ours, the last person to leave walks a fixed route through the building: down the corridor past the copier, through the glass door into the open-plan floor, and finally into the little kitchen where the kettle lives. Along the way there are plants to water on Mondays and Thursdays, a whiteboard to wipe if anyone has been sketching diagrams, and a stack of parcels that the mail room leaves by the stairs. The ritual matters more than it sounds. When the route is skipped, something always goes wrong: a window left open in the rain, a printer humming all night, a fridge door standing ajar. So the team agreed years ago that whoever leaves last takes the walk, and nobody argues about whose turn it is. I have done it hundreds of times now, and I could probably manage it in the dark. The corridor lights go dark behind me, one sensor at a time. In the kitchen I rinse my mug, set it on the rack, and read again the notice above the sink: please turn off the lights and lock the back door before you leave the building. There is a notice taped to the inside of the door that says exactly that, in capitals, because the previous office manager was fond of capitals. Outside, the street is quiet, the bakery across the road is closing its shutters, and the bus stop glows under its own small lamp. On winter evenings the walk home is cold and quick, and I am usually asleep before the kettle has finished cooling.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A same-length long passage with the baseline 'turn off' deep inside, so a rule that reads only probe length cannot account for the long holdout's result.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Off went the alarm the moment the back door opened.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The token ' off' in sentence-initial position, where the hypothesis predicts baseline and where a first-token floor may or may not be measured.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Medical staff will section the tissue samples during the night shift.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'section' as part of the verb 'sectioned', a part-of-speech change with the token kept but no 'cross' frame, which the hypothesis says is baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Our team built a well-known text-decoration library for email templates.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Three compound second elements ('-known', '-decoration', and ' email') that carry no severance meaning, which the subword-compound rival predicts will fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The budget cut forced the department to cancel two planned hires.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'cut' as a noun with no particle, inside the hypothesis's acknowledged near-baseline band for the bare 'cut' token, testing frame completion rather than the token alone.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: 由于大雨，比赛中断了将近两个小时才重新开始。
adversarial_test_results.detail: Chinese 中断, which the hypothesis explicitly calls baseline; the tokenizer yields '比赛中' + '断', so the bare claimed token '断' appears but not after the '中' of 中断, isolating the context claim from the token claim.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: 根据医生的诊断，他只是得了一场轻微的感冒。
adversarial_test_results.detail: 诊断 tokenizes as a single word, so the claimed token '断' never appears and the hypothesis and all three rivals predict baseline; it corrects the earlier assumption that 断 was a separate subword piece.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The little magazine began in a borrowed room above a bicycle shop. Its founders had no money and very little experience, but they had a mimeograph machine, a list of names, and an unreasonable amount of energy. The first issue ran to sixteen pages and was stapled by hand on a kitchen table. Most of the copies went to friends, a few went to bookshops that agreed to stock them on consignment, and one went to a librarian in another city who wrote back with two pages of careful notes. That letter kept the project alive through its difficult second year. The editors learned as they went: how to proofread, how to beg favours from printers, how to design a cover that would survive the post. They published essays, interviews, translations, drawings, and the occasional poem that nobody could quite explain. Circulation grew slowly, then quickly, and by the fifth year the magazine had subscribers in several countries. What never changed was the rule the founders set at the very beginning: every issue would include at least one new voice. In the autumn issue, between an interview with a retired lighthouse keeper and a set of photographs of the harbour at dawn, he published a short story about a boy who collects lost keys, and it was that piece, more than anything else in those early years, that readers still mention when they write to the editors.

readings.explanation: Severance-phrase detector: the positive pole fires on the token that completes an expression of cutting or severing, above all the particle ' off' (or the closed forms 'cutoff'/'cut-off'/'cutoffs'/'crosscut') when the verb is a form of cut (4.9-8.4 of the 6.1 max), and more weakly after other blade or detachment verbs such as chop, clip, trim, slice, crop, hack, lop, snip, sever, rip, tear, break, bite, chip, snap, twist, chew, crush, slash or mince (1.4-4.1, but not saw/prune/shave/peel/amputate off); the same completing role is played by ' short' after cut ('cut it short', 3.8), the ' section'/' sections' of 'cross section'/'cross-sectional' (3.3-3.7), and Chinese severance words (截止 3.1-6.0, 截 4.1, 截断 6.6, 截取 3.7, 割断 2.7, 剪断 1.8). The same tokens outside such a frame stay near baseline (<1.0: ' off' after turn/take/set/pay/sign/log/call/push/lift/wash/peel, 'a short story', 'the section of the report', 停止/结束/中断), while the object slot right after cut already reads 1.9 ('cut it') and 2.7 when 'Cut' opens the text, so only activity above about 2 is severance-specific.

Narrow reading: the pole is keyed to the single English verb 'cut' plus its particle 'off' (and closed forms cutoff/cut-off), so it should fire on 'cut ... off' anywhere but not on chop/clip/trim/slice + off, 截止/截断, or 'cross section'.

Collocation-memory reading: the pole merely completes any frequent fixed two-word unit already begun in context (cut off, cross section, cut short, of course, New York), so it is phrase memory rather than severance and should fire on 'course' after 'of' and 'York' after 'New'.

Subword-compound reading: the pole fires on the second element of any compound word or non-initial subword piece regardless of meaning (off in cut-off, section in cross-section, Short in moduleShortSuffix, pt in ceptor), so it should fire equally on well-known, e-mail and text-decoration.
